html:
A Buddhist stupa, a domed mound over relics, on a hilltop at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh, India. The emperor Ashoka began it in the 3rd century BCE as a brick dome.

About a century later it was enlarged and faced with stone. In the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE, under the Satavahanas, four tall stone gateways, the toranas, were added at the points of the compass. Their carvings tell stories of the Buddha's life and past lives. In the oldest of them the Buddha himself is never shown in human form; a tree, a wheel, a throne or footprints stand for him.

Ivory carvers of nearby Vidisha paid for part of the work, as an inscription records. The site stayed in use for over a thousand years, then was abandoned and forgotten. A British officer found it in 1818. Today it is a World Heritage Site and one of the best kept groups of early Buddhist monuments, alongside the Ajanta caves. Its gateway forms appear in Buddhist building from India to East Asia.
